title: Reverse Periodization for Improving Sports Performance: A Systematic Review
authors: González-Ravé JM, González-Mohino F, Rodrigo-Carranza V, Pyne DB
population: Athletes in 11 studies (swimming, running, muscular endurance, strength, VO2max outcomes)
findings: 925 studies identified, 17 remained after screening and 11 were included, with 200 athletes in total.
Reverse periodization did not provide superior performance improvements in swimming, running, muscular endurance, maximum strength or maximal oxygen uptake versus traditional or block periodization.
Evidence level was 1b (individual RCT) for two investigations and 2b (individual cohort) for the remainder; mean PEDro 4.9 (range 0-7).
Reverse periodization appears no more effective than other forms; more comparative studies are needed across a range of endurance sports.
limitations: Small number of moderate-to-low quality studies across mixed sports; few running studies and none on ultra-distance events.
implications: Do not make reverse periodization (intensity first, volume later) a default; use a traditional base-build-specific-taper sequence.
Allow reverse sequencing only as a user-selected option and make no performance-benefit claim.

verification.notes: Crossref and PubMed match (Sports Med Open 2022;8(1):56). Added 17-remaining-studies detail. Evidence level downgraded A to B because of low-moderate primary-study quality (PEDro 4.9).
